sizeRange.notes: North America's largest salamander; record individuals exceed 24 inches

description: North America's largest salamander and one of only three giant salamander species in the world, the eastern hellbender is a fully aquatic species found in the clean, cold, fast-flowing rivers of Virginia's mountains. They breathe primarily through folds of skin along their sides and require highly oxygenated water. Their populations have declined sharply due to water quality degradation and sedimentation. Finding a hellbender while fishing or snorkeling is a sign of an exceptionally healthy river.
identificationFeatures: Enormous size, 11.5–24+ inches — unmistakable
Flattened head and body
Fleshy skin folds along the sides
Brown with darker mottling, no bright colors
Small eyes, fully aquatic
Found only in fast, rocky mountain streams

similarSpecies.differentiator: Mudpuppies are much smaller with visible bushy red external gills; hellbenders are far larger and have no external gills as adults

funFact: Hellbenders are sometimes called 'snot otters,' 'devil dogs,' or 'Allegheny alligators' by anglers — and are completely harmless. They actually compete with trout for crayfish, not with anglers for fish.
sercNotes: VWAP Tier Ia. If found as bycatch by a fisher or encountered in distress, contact Virginia DWR immediately. Do not remove from the water.

description: Virginia's most commonly seen salamander, the red-spotted newt has a remarkable three-stage life cycle. Aquatic larvae transform into terrestrial red efts — vivid orange-red juveniles that wander forest floors for up to seven years before returning to water as olive-green aquatic adults. The bright orange eft stage is a warning coloration: newts produce tetrodotoxin, a potent neurotoxin, in their skin.
identificationFeatures: Eft stage (juvenile, terrestrial): bright orange-red with a row of red spots bordered by black along the sides
Adult stage (aquatic): olive-green or yellowish-brown with red spots bordered by black
Small to medium size, 2.25–4.8 inches
Rough, granular skin in eft stage; smoother in adult stage
Compressed tail in adult stage for swimming

similarSpecies.differentiator: Red salamanders are plethodontids (lungless salamanders) without the red eft's distinct bordered spots; they lack the newt's compressed swimming tail

funFact: Red efts are toxic enough that a single newt contains enough tetrodotoxin to kill several adult humans — making them one of the most toxic vertebrates in North America despite their small size.

description: One of Virginia's most spectacular amphibians, the spotted salamander is a large, stocky species that spends most of its life underground in hardwood forests. On the first warm rainy nights of late winter or early spring, hundreds may migrate to vernal pools to breed in a brief explosive event. The vivid yellow or orange spots on a black body make them unmistakable.
identificationFeatures: Large, 6–9.8 inches
Black or dark gray above with two irregular rows of yellow or orange spots from head to tail
Spots on the head often more orange; spots on the body more yellow
Stout, rounded body
Yellow belly

similarSpecies.differentiator: Marbled salamanders have white or silver bands on black rather than yellow spots; they breed in fall rather than early spring

funFact: Spotted salamander eggs contain symbiotic algae that live inside the egg capsules — the algae produce oxygen from photosynthesis that the developing embryos use, and the embryos produce carbon dioxide that the algae use.

description: A strikingly patterned, stocky salamander of Virginia's forests, the marbled salamander is unique among Virginia's mole salamanders in that it breeds in fall rather than spring. Females guard egg clutches in dry depressions until autumn rains fill the vernal pool. The bold white or silver crossbands on a black body make it one of Virginia's most distinctive salamanders.
identificationFeatures: Black body with white or silver crossbands
Bands more silvery in males, whiter in females
Stout, heavy-bodied
Medium size, 3.5–5 inches
Terrestrial, found under logs and in leaf litter

similarSpecies.differentiator: Spotted salamanders have rows of yellow or orange spots, not white crossbands; they breed in early spring while marbled salamanders breed in fall

funFact: Female marbled salamanders are unusually devoted parents for amphibians — they coil around their egg clutch for weeks in fall, protecting it from predators and keeping it moist until rains flood the nest site.

description: The eastern red-backed salamander is Virginia's most abundant salamander and likely the most abundant terrestrial vertebrate in many of its forests by sheer biomass. Entirely terrestrial and lungless — they breathe through their moist skin — they are found under nearly every log and flat rock in suitable forest habitat. They come in two color morphs: the red-backed morph with a brick-red stripe, and the lead-backed morph which is entirely dark gray.
identificationFeatures: Small, slender, 2.25–4 inches
Red-backed morph: broad brick-red or orange-red stripe down the back with straight-edged sides
Lead-backed morph: uniformly dark gray with no stripe — same species
Salt-and-pepper pattern on belly — black and white flecking
No spots or other markings

similarSpecies.differentiator: Slimy salamanders are larger, black with white or silver spots, and produce a sticky mucus; red-backed salamanders are smaller with a plain stripe or lead coloring
Red efts are brighter orange with bordered black spots; red-backed salamanders have a duller stripe with plain edges and a salt-and-pepper belly

funFact: Eastern red-backed salamanders are lungless — they breathe entirely through their skin and the lining of their mouth. This means they must stay moist at all times and are highly sensitive to drought and pollution.

description: A large, glossy black salamander with white or silver spots and flecks, the northern slimy salamander is common in Virginia's forests under logs and in rock crevices. True to its name, it produces a thick, sticky mucus from its skin that is notoriously difficult to wash off — it was historically used as a substitute for glue. Like all plethodontids, it is lungless.
identificationFeatures: Large for a plethodontid, 4.75–6.75 inches
Glossy black above with scattered white or silver spots and flecks
Dark gray or black belly
Produces very sticky skin secretions
Stout body

similarSpecies.differentiator: Red-backed salamanders are smaller with a red stripe or lead-gray coloring, not black with white spots
Spotted salamanders are mole salamanders (Ambystomatidae) with rounder bodies, yellow spots, and are associated with vernal pools; slimy salamanders are slenderer plethodontids with white spots

funFact: The sticky secretion of slimy salamanders was once actually used as glue — it bonds strongly to skin and many surfaces and requires soap and repeated washing to remove.

description: A slender, yellow or orange-brown salamander with two dark lines running down the back, the northern two-lined salamander is one of Virginia's most commonly encountered stream salamanders. They are found under rocks along stream edges and seepages throughout the state. Their bright coloring and slender proportions make them easy to identify.
identificationFeatures: Slender body, 2.5–4.75 inches
Yellow, orange, or greenish-yellow above
Two dark lines or rows of spots running from eye to tail
Yellow or orange belly
Found under streamside rocks and in seeps

similarSpecies.differentiator: Long-tailed salamanders have a proportionally very long tail (more than half total length) with a herringbone pattern; two-lined salamanders have a shorter tail and plainer striping

funFact: Two-lined salamander larvae can take up to three years to metamorphose in cold mountain streams — they spend years as aquatic larvae breathing through feathery external gills before transforming into adults.

description: A large, permanently aquatic salamander found in Virginia's rivers and larger streams, the mudpuppy is neotenic — it retains its larval features, including bushy red external gills, throughout its entire life and never metamorphoses. They are nocturnal and secretive, hiding under large rocks and debris in deeper water. Despite being fairly common, they are rarely seen.
identificationFeatures: Large, 8–17 inches
Bushy, dark red external gills — present throughout life
Dark brown or gray with darker spots
Stout, flattened body with four short legs
Fully aquatic — never leaves the water

similarSpecies.differentiator: Hellbenders are much larger with no external gills and extensive skin folds; mudpuppies are smaller with distinctive bushy red gills

funFact: Mudpuppies are often caught by fishermen and are sometimes killed out of fear — they are completely harmless and are actually an indicator of healthy river water quality.

description: A small, delicate salamander of sphagnum bogs and moist forested wetlands, the four-toed salamander is the only Virginia salamander with four toes on the hind foot rather than the usual five. They nest in moss above water, and females often nest communally. The bright white belly with distinct black spots and the constriction at the base of the tail are distinctive.
identificationFeatures: Small, 2–4 inches
Reddish-brown above, sometimes with gray flecking
White belly with distinct black spots — very clean, high-contrast pattern
Visible constriction at base of tail
Four toes on hind feet instead of the usual five — requires close examination

similarSpecies.differentiator: Red-backed salamanders have five toes on hind feet and a salt-and-pepper belly without distinct black spots; four-toed salamanders have a clean white belly with black spots

funFact: If grabbed by a predator, four-toed salamanders can voluntarily drop their tail at the constriction point — the tail continues to wriggle, distracting the predator while the salamander escapes.

description: One of Virginia's most common stream-edge salamanders, the northern dusky salamander is found under rocks and debris along the margins of springs, seeps, and small streams. They are variable in color and can be difficult to distinguish from related dusky salamander species, but the light line from eye to jaw and the keeled tail are consistent features.
identificationFeatures: Light line from the back of the eye to the angle of the jaw
Keeled (ridged) tail — laterally compressed and knife-edged
Variable brown, gray, or tan above, often with a dorsal pattern that fades with age
Medium size, 2.5–5.5 inches
Found under rocks at stream edges and seeps

similarSpecies.differentiator: Two-lined salamanders are brighter yellow or orange with two distinct dark lines; dusky salamanders are browner and have a keeled tail and the eye-to-jaw light line

funFact: Dusky salamanders have unusually strong hind legs relative to their body size, which allows them to jump impressively for a salamander — a behavior used to escape predators at stream edges.
